pat.duty-on-one-link-in-a-chain.fix: Extend the duty to controlling persons and intermediaries, or add a rule making them answerable for evasion.
pat.election-into-a-lighter-parallel-reg: A party can choose to register or qualify under a second law that places lighter duties on it.
Find other laws under which a party could register or qualify with lighter duties. Ask whether this bill addresses that choice.
State which set of rules governs when more than one applies, and bar a party from choosing the lighter set for the same activity.
pat.timing-moves-around-a-date.plain: Parties can move transactions across an effective date or holding period.
pat.timing-moves-around-a-date.check: Find effective dates and holding periods. Ask whether transactions could be moved across them, and whether a look back rule (which examines earlier transactions) or a rule against timing transactions exists.
pat.timing-moves-around-a-date.fix: Add a look back period (a span of earlier time that is examined) and a rule disregarding transactions timed mainly to fall on the favorable side of a date.
pat.netting-that-cancels-a-charge.plain: Offset rules, which subtract credits, can reduce a new tax or duty toward zero.
pat.netting-that-cancels-a-charge.check: Find offset, credit and netting rules (rules that subtract one amount from another) attached to a new charge or duty. Ask whether they could reduce it toward zero.
pat.netting-that-cancels-a-charge.fix: Cap the offsets, or set a minimum amount that netting cannot reduce.
pat.offsetting-response-by-another-gover: A state or other government can redesign its own law to cancel out the effect of the federal limit.
Find limits placed on another level of government. Ask whether that government could redesign its own law to cancel out the limit, and whether the bill's text anticipates that.
Add a rule that addresses offsetting changes by other governments, and a duty to report on those changes so they can be tracked.
pat.single-enforcer.plain: Only one federal agency may enforce the law, and state attorneys general have no parallel authority to enforce it.
pat.single-enforcer.check: Find who may enforce the bill. Ask whether state officials or others have parallel authority, and what happens if the one enforcer does not act.
pat.single-enforcer.fix: Give state officials parallel enforcement authority, and allow a private right of action as an additional way to enforce.
pat.no-reward-for-insiders.plain: The bill at most protects whistleblowers and offers no relator suit (a suit by a private person for the government) or bounty (a share of money recovered).
pat.no-reward-for-insiders.check: Look for protection, rewards or the right to sue for insiders who report violations. Ask whether reporting carries any benefit beyond protection from retaliation.
pat.no-reward-for-insiders.fix: Add a right for insiders to report violations with a share of the money recovered, and add protection from retaliation.
pat.private-right-without-economics.plai: A right to sue exists, but the bill gives no fixed or multiplied damages and no way to recover legal fees, so small claims are not worth bringing.
pat.private-right-without-economics.chec: Find any right to sue and read the remedies. Ask whether damages, multiples of damages or shifting of legal fees to the losing side make a small claim worth bringing.
pat.private-right-without-economics.fix: Add fixed or multiplied damages, and let a plaintiff who wins recover reasonable legal fees.
pat.fees-lost-on-voluntary-compliance.pl: Fee shifting applies only to judgments, so a defendant can comply after being sued and avoid paying fees.
pat.fees-lost-on-voluntary-compliance.ch: Read the fee shifting terms. Ask whether fees are available only after a judgment, and whether a defendant could comply after being sued and avoid them.
pat.fees-lost-on-voluntary-compliance.fi: Allow fees where the lawsuit led to the change in conduct, not only after a judgment.
pat.non-enforcement-left-unreviewable.pl: No standards or triggers say when the agency must enforce. As a result, a decision not to enforce, including a decision covering a whole category of cases, cannot be challenged.
pat.non-enforcement-left-unreviewable.ch: Find the standards for when the agency must enforce. Ask whether a decision not to enforce, including one covering a whole category of cases, can be challenged.
pat.non-enforcement-left-unreviewable.fi: State criteria or triggers for enforcement, allow review of a refusal to enforce, and add a duty to report.
pat.statutory-damages-without-concrete-h: Fixed damages for a bare violation, meaning one with no proven harm, leave many plaintiffs without standing (the right to sue) in federal court.
Find fixed damages for a bare violation, meaning a violation with no proven harm. Ask whether a plaintiff must show concrete harm to sue in federal court, and which plaintiffs would be left out.
Define the injury that the fixed damages provision addresses, allow other enforcers to sue, and provide an alternative forum.
pat.agency-penalties-without-a-court-pat: Civil penalties can be imposed only in the agency's own tribunal, and that arrangement is open to a challenge claiming a right to a jury trial.
Find civil penalties imposed in the agency's own tribunal. Ask whether a route through the courts exists, and whether a challenge claiming a right to a jury trial could stall them.
Provide a court action for penalties as an alternative to the agency's tribunal.
pat.funding-conditions-without-rights-la: Duties are written as conditions on grants without clear terms creating rights, so the people the grants are meant to help cannot sue.
Find duties written as conditions on grants. Ask whether the text uses clear language creating rights, and whether the people who benefit could sue.
Use express language that creates rights, and state who may enforce it.
pat.independence-resting-on-removal-prot: The design assumes that the officials who enforce the law cannot be removed at will.
Find protections that assume enforcers cannot be removed at will. Ask what happens to the design if a court finds those protections invalid.
Add a substitute structure that keeps the body's function if removal protection is invalidated.
pat.missing-clear-statement-on-states.pl: The bill changes the balance of power between the federal government and the states, or subjects states to lawsuits, without the explicit statement that courts require.
pat.missing-clear-statement-on-states.ch: Find provisions that change the balance between the federal government and the states or that subject states to suit. Ask whether the text says so explicitly, in the way courts require.
pat.missing-clear-statement-on-states.fi: State the intended effect on state governments in clear, express terms.
pat.mental-state-unstated-or-set-high.pl: A penalty provision says nothing about the violator's mental state, or liability attaches only to "willful" or "knowing" violations.
pat.mental-state-unstated-or-set-high.ch: Find penalty provisions and read the mental state they require, meaning what the violator must have known or intended. Ask whether it is unstated, or limited to 'willful' or 'knowing' acts, and what a regulated party could claim not to know.
pat.mental-state-unstated-or-set-high.fi: State the required mental state, and provide for civil liability without proof of intent.
pat.ambiguity-in-a-penalty-provision.pla: Unclear words in a provision carrying criminal penalties are read in the defendant's favor, and that reading can also be applied in civil cases.
pat.ambiguity-in-a-penalty-provision.che: Find unclear words in provisions carrying criminal penalties. Ask whether the narrower reading would be applied, and whether that reading could also be applied in civil cases.
pat.ambiguity-in-a-penalty-provision.fix: Define the key terms of any penalty provision, and separate the civil standard from the criminal standard.
pat.narrowing-by-constitutional-doubt.pl: A party can win a narrow reading of a law by raising a serious constitutional question, even without winning the constitutional claim itself.
pat.narrowing-by-constitutional-doubt.ch: Find provisions that could raise a serious constitutional question. Ask whether a court could adopt a narrow reading to avoid it.
pat.narrowing-by-constitutional-doubt.fi: Include a clear statement of how broadly the provision is meant to apply, and findings that support the provision.
pat.gates-on-private-suits.plain: A mandatory notice period, a bar while the government is "diligently prosecuting" (actively pursuing its own case), or a government power to dismiss can stop a private suit.
pat.gates-on-private-suits.check: Find notice periods, bars on suits while the government is prosecuting, and government powers to dismiss. Ask whether any of them could stop a private suit before it proceeds.
pat.gates-on-private-suits.fix: Limit the notice period, define when a government action blocks a private suit, and require court approval of dismissals.
pat.private-relator-open-to-challenge.pl: Enforcement by relators, who sue on the government's behalf, faces unresolved objections under Article II of the Constitution.
pat.private-relator-open-to-challenge.ch: Find enforcement by private parties on the government's behalf. Ask what constitutional objections could be raised and what happens if they succeed.
pat.private-relator-open-to-challenge.fi: Add a government enforcement path that continues if the system of suits by private relators is invalidated.
pat.past-violations-not-actionable.plain: Private suits reach only ongoing or future violations, or only relief that looks forward.
pat.past-violations-not-actionable.check: Read what private suits may reach. Ask whether past violations can be sued over or only ongoing ones, and whether only relief that applies to the future is available.
pat.past-violations-not-actionable.fix: Allow suits over past violations within a stated period, and provide for damages as well as relief that applies to the future.
pat.limitation-period-that-never-restart: The limitation period, which is the time allowed to sue, runs from the first act and does not restart with each continuing effect.
Find limitation periods, meaning deadlines to sue, and when each one starts. Ask whether each continuing effect restarts the deadline or only the first act counts.
State that each continuing violation or new effect starts a new limitation period.
pat.no-time-limit-on-rule-challenges.pla: The bill relies on the general six-year time limit, which restarts for each newly injured party.
pat.no-time-limit-on-rule-challenges.che: Look for a time limit on challenges to rules made under the bill. Ask whether the general default time limit applies and when it restarts.
pat.no-time-limit-on-rule-challenges.fix: State a specific filing period for challenges, and state when it starts.
pat.filing-rule-readable-as-jurisdiction: A deadline or precondition is worded so that a court treats it as a limit on its own power, not as a rule that can be waived.
Find deadlines and preconditions to suit. Ask whether the wording could be read as a limit on the court's power instead of a rule that can be waived.
Word deadlines as claim processing rules, which are ordinary procedural rules, and state that they may be waived or tolled (paused).
pat.private-trigger-open-to-misuse.plain: A private notice or complaint can force action, but the bill sets no penalty for false notices, no counter-notice and too little time to verify.
pat.private-trigger-open-to-misuse.check: Find private notices or complaints that compel action. Ask what penalizes false ones, whether a counter notice process exists, and whether the time allowed to verify them is enough.
pat.private-trigger-open-to-misuse.fix: Add a penalty for false notices, a counter notice process and a reasonable period for verification.
pat.enforcement-gated-by-a-vote-or-limit: A penalty requires a political vote before it applies, or recovery is limited to profit that the violator actually realized.
Find penalties that need a vote before they apply, and recovery limited to realized profit. Ask who controls the vote and whether the cap makes a violation inexpensive for the violator.
Remove the vote requirement, and allow recovery beyond profit, such as damages or fixed penalties.
pat.dollar-figures-not-indexed.plain: Penalties, caps and thresholds are fixed dollar amounts that lose value or drift as inflation changes prices.
pat.dollar-figures-not-indexed.check: List each fixed dollar penalty, cap and threshold. Ask whether it is indexed (adjusted automatically for inflation), and what it will be worth after several years of inflation.
pat.dollar-figures-not-indexed.fix: Index dollar figures to a named measure with a scheduled adjustment.
pat.penalties-deductible-or-untracked.pl: Nothing in the bill bars penalties from being deducted, and nothing says where penalty money goes.
pat.penalties-deductible-or-untracked.ch: Find how the bill treats penalty payments. Ask whether they can be deducted or recovered from others, and where the money goes.
pat.penalties-deductible-or-untracked.fi: Bar the deduction of penalties, and direct where penalty receipts are deposited and reported.
pat.appropriated-funds-can-be-withheld.p: Money is appropriated, but nothing forces it to be committed for spending on time, and nothing lets anyone sue if it is held back.
pat.appropriated-funds-can-be-withheld.c: Find appropriations (money set aside by law for spending) and ask whether anything forces the money to be committed on time. Ask whether anyone can sue if the money is held back.
pat.appropriated-funds-can-be-withheld.f: Add a deadline for committing the funds, and a duty to report on delays.
pat.funding-that-depends-on-a-request.pl: Mandatory funding is paid only when the agency head asks for it or a contested formula term is met.
pat.funding-that-depends-on-a-request.ch: Find funding that is paid only on a request or when a formula term is met. Ask who controls the request, and what happens if no one makes it.
pat.funding-that-depends-on-a-request.fi: Provide funding by default, with the request or formula acting as an adjustment rather than a condition.
pat.offsets-that-score-without-changing-: Changes to mandatory programs, or repeated delay of a rule that was never in force, are counted as savings.
Find savings used to pay for new spending. Ask whether they change actual outlays (money actually spent), or merely count the delay of a rule that was never in force.
Report the savings and the basis for counting them, and require a review of actual outlays.
pat.designations-and-timing-shifts-outsi: Emergency designations, advance appropriations and timing shifts take spending outside budget limits.
Find emergency designations, advance appropriations and timing shifts. Ask whether they move spending outside budget limits.
Require a stated justification for each designation, and report the totals measured against the budget limits.
pat.spending-authority-outside-appropria: Contract or borrowing authority lets funds be committed without an appropriation.
Find contract or borrowing authority. Ask whether it commits funds without an appropriation, and who reviews the commitments.
Require an appropriation, or a reporting and review step, before any commitment is made.
pat.provision-shaped-to-a-reconciliation: A provision is sized, given an end date or worded to meet the Senate's Byrd rule on budget reconciliation bills.
Find provisions sized, dated or worded to meet a special budget procedure. Ask whether the provision's form departs from what the policy would otherwise need.
Disclose which provisions were shaped for the procedure, and review them after they become law.
pat.serial-short-term-renewal.plain: Temporary provisions are renewed repeatedly instead of being made permanent or ended.
pat.serial-short-term-renewal.check: Find temporary provisions and their expiry dates. Ask whether they have been renewed before, and whether making them permanent or ending them is an option.
pat.serial-short-term-renewal.fix: Set a longer term, or a review that leads to a decision to make the provision permanent or to end it.
pat.mandate-silent-on-who-pays.plain: A requirement is imposed without saying which party bears its cost.
pat.mandate-silent-on-who-pays.check: Find each requirement and ask which party bears its cost. Check whether the text says so, and ask what happens if that party cannot pay.
pat.mandate-silent-on-who-pays.fix: State who bears the cost and how, with funding or cost sharing where needed.
Two programs pay for the same period or need with no coordination clause.
Find programs that pay for the same period or need. Ask whether a clause coordinates them, and whether double payment is possible.
Add a coordination clause that provides for an offset or a priority between the programs.
pat.amendatory-instruction-that-cannot-b: An instruction to strike, insert or renumber words in an existing law is ambiguous or does not match the text it amends.
Check each instruction to strike, insert or renumber text against the text it amends. Ask whether it can be carried out exactly as written.
Verify each instruction against the current text of the amended law before the bill becomes law.
pat.reference-inside-amendatory-text-to-: Inside quoted inserted text, "this Act" or "the date of enactment of this Act" refers to the amended law, not the new bill.
Read quoted inserted text for the phrases 'this Act' and 'date of enactment of this Act'. Ask whether each points to the amended law or to the new bill.
Name the intended law and date expressly inside the inserted text.
A bill amends the Code for a title that is not positive law, or amends the Act for a title that is positive law.
Check whether each amendment targets the Code or the Act, and whether the title is positive law. Ask whether the citation form fits the title.
Use the correct citation form for each title and confirm it with the codifiers.
pat.broken-circular-or-chained-cross-ref: A reference points to the wrong part of the law, to itself, or to a series of other references.
Follow each cross-reference to its target. Ask whether it points to the right part of the law, to itself, or through a chain of other references.
Replace chained references with direct ones and check that each target exists.
pat.repeal-or-sunset-with-unintended-sur: A repeal does not bring back the prior law, and a sunset (an end date for an authority) leaves the amendments the Act made in force.
Read each repeal and sunset. Ask whether prior law returns, and whether amendments made by the Act stay in force after the authority ends.
State which provisions and amendments end, and whether earlier law is restored.
pat.repeal-silent-on-accrued-liabilities: A repeal or expiry does not say whether penalties already incurred survive, so the general savings statute decides the question.
Read each repeal or expiry for how it treats penalties already incurred. Ask whether they survive or whether the general savings rule decides.
State whether accrued penalties and pending cases continue after repeal or expiry.
pat.effective-date-confused-with-applica: The bill does not distinguish the date the text takes effect from the persons, things or events it applies to.
Find each effective date. Ask whether the text separates the date it takes effect from the persons, things and events it applies to.
State the effective date and the rule on who or what the bill applies to in separate provisions.
pat.no-transitional-rules.plain: The bill changes current programs or behavior without saying how existing cases move to the new rule.
pat.no-transitional-rules.check: Look for rules on how existing cases, contracts and programs move to the new rule. Ask what happens to those in progress on the effective date.
pat.no-transitional-rules.fix: Add transitional provisions covering pending matters and a schedule for existing cases.
pat.substantive-rule-stranded-in-an-amen: A free-standing rule sits in an amending or temporary section, where it will not be codified (placed in the official Code) with the parent law.
Find free standing rules in amending or temporary sections. Ask whether they will be codified with the parent law and whether readers will find them.
Place the rule in the parent law or state how it is to be codified.
pat.restatement-of-other-law.plain: A provision repeats existing law, which creates two sources of the same rule that can diverge.
pat.restatement-of-other-law.check: Find provisions repeating existing law. Ask whether the two sources could diverge, and which one governs if they do.
pat.restatement-of-other-law.fix: Cross-refer to the existing law instead of restating it, or state which text governs.
pat.conflict-with-international-obligati: The measure conflicts with a treaty or trade commitment, and general language saying the measure overrides other law does not reach that conflict.
Compare the measure with treaty and trade commitments. Ask whether any conflict exists, and whether general language overriding other law reaches it.
Add an express statement on the relationship to those obligations and a review step.
pat.boilerplate-relied-on-for-work-it-do: Stock phrases such as a general override or a routine severability clause, which keeps the rest of a law in force if part is struck down, are treated as protective.
Find standard clauses such as a general override or a severability clause. Ask whether they actually protect what the drafters think they protect.
Replace boilerplate with specific text where protection matters, such as named provisions or tailored severability.
pat.no-protection-from-later-implied-ove: Nothing requires a later law to refer expressly to this bill before replacing it.
Look for any rule that requires a later law to refer expressly to this bill before replacing it. Ask whether a later law could override this bill silently.
Add a clause requiring any later law that would displace this bill to refer to it expressly.
pat.no-fallback-if-struck-down.plain: No substitute rule takes effect if a court invalidates the primary provision.
pat.no-fallback-if-struck-down.check: Find the primary provision and ask what applies if a court invalidates it. Ask whether any substitute takes effect.
pat.no-fallback-if-struck-down.fix: Add a fallback rule that takes effect if the primary provision is invalidated.
Provisions enacted as a package are not made inseverable, meaning tied so that they stand or fall together, so a court can remove one of the linked provisions.
Find provisions enacted as a package or bargain. Ask whether the text makes them inseverable, and what remains if a court removes one of them.
State which provisions stand or fall together and add a fallback.
pat.no-fast-track-for-validity-challenge: Constitutional challenges follow ordinary procedure, so the law's status stays uncertain for years.
Look for expedited procedure for constitutional challenges. Ask how long the law's status could stay uncertain under ordinary procedure.
Provide expedited review, a single forum and direct appeal for validity challenges.
pat.savings-clause-that-does-not-stop-im: A clause preserving state law does not prevent a finding of conflict preemption (federal law displacing state law that conflicts with it), and loose terms such as "requirements" can reach common-law claims.

Read each clause preserving state law. Ask whether it stops a finding of conflict preemption, and whether words such as 'requirements' reach common law claims, which are claims based on court-made law.
Add an express statement that conflict preemption does not apply to preserved state law, and define 'requirements'.
pat.preemption-without-a-replacement-sta: State rules are displaced, but the federal government sets no replacement standard, so no regulation applies.
Find provisions displacing state rules. Ask what federal standard replaces them, and what level of regulation remains.
Pair displacement with a federal standard, or limit displacement to areas that the federal rule covers.
pat.funding-conditions-that-deter-state-: Grant eligibility is used to discourage state or local regulation.
Find grant eligibility terms that concern state or local regulation. Ask whether they discourage governments from adopting their own rules.
Limit conditions to how the funds are used, and state that eligibility does not depend on giving up state rules.
pat.no-anti-backsliding-rule.plain: Standards, permits or plans can be revised downward at renewal, and no minimum level prevents it.
pat.no-anti-backsliding-rule.check: Find provisions for revising standards, permits or plans. Ask whether any minimum level prevents a downward revision at renewal.
pat.no-anti-backsliding-rule.fix: Add a rule that a revision may not be less protective than the existing standard unless a finding is stated.
pat.no-construction-rule-for-coverage.pl: No instruction says that coverage terms are to be read broadly to serve the bill's purpose.
pat.no-construction-rule-for-coverage.ch: Look for an instruction on how broadly coverage terms are to be read. Ask whether a narrow reading would defeat the bill's stated purpose.
pat.no-construction-rule-for-coverage.fi: Add a rule that coverage terms are to be read in the way that serves the bill's purpose, and state exceptions narrowly.
pat.later-ratification-of-a-lenient-read: Reenactment without change lets a party argue that Congress accepted a narrow reading by an agency or court.
Find provisions reenacted without change after an agency or court read them narrowly. Ask whether a party could argue that the legislature accepted that reading.
State in the text that reenactment does not approve any prior reading.
pat.orphaned-functions-after-a-sunset.pl: The administering body expires while its contracts, licenses or fee collections continue, and no successor is named.
pat.orphaned-functions-after-a-sunset.ch: Find bodies that expire, and ask what happens to their contracts, licenses and fee collections. Ask whether a successor is named.
pat.orphaned-functions-after-a-sunset.fi: Name a successor body and provide for the transfer of functions when an agency ends under a sunset.
pat.no-authority-to-correct-a-known-flaw: The agency cannot fix an acknowledged error or distortion without new legislation.
Look for authority to fix an acknowledged error without new legislation. Ask what the agency could do if a flaw appears.
Add a limited correction authority with notice, a stated finding and a reporting duty.
pat.eligibility-by-self-attestation.plai: A benefit or status is established by the applicant's own statement, and verification is barred or not required.
pat.eligibility-by-self-attestation.chec: Find benefits or status established by the applicant's own statement. Ask whether verification is allowed, barred or required.
pat.eligibility-by-self-attestation.fix: Allow verification and audit of attestations (applicants' own statements) after the fact, with penalties for false statements.
pat.bar-on-sharing-data-between-agencies: A law's wording or silence stops one agency from giving another agency the data it needs.
Read confidentiality and privacy language. Ask whether it stops one agency from giving another the data it needs to carry out the bill.
Add an express data sharing authority, with safeguards.
pat.decision-rule-decoupled-from-its-dri: A decision is separated in time from the choices that make it necessary, and inaction produces an outcome that no one intends.
Find decisions set apart in time from the choices that make them necessary. Ask what happens if no one acts, and whether that result is intended.
Set a default outcome that matches the intended policy and require a decision before the default applies.
pat.no-backstop-for-delegated-implemente: States or other delegates carry out the program, and nothing provides for the federal government to act in their place if they do not.
Find programs carried out by states or other delegates. Ask what happens if a delegate does not act, and whether a default exists, meaning a rule under which the federal government acts instead.
Provide a federal default or takeover if the delegate does not carry out the program.
pat.no-scheduled-review-of-standards.pla: Standards are set once and coverage shrinks as conditions change.
pat.no-scheduled-review-of-standards.che: Look for a review date for standards set in the bill. Ask whether coverage could shrink as conditions change.
pat.no-scheduled-review-of-standards.fix: Add a scheduled review with a duty to update and report.
pat.review-duty-with-a-built-in-exit.pla: A periodic review or report can be skipped on the agency's own decision.
pat.review-duty-with-a-built-in-exit.che: Find periodic reviews and reports. Ask whether the agency may skip them on its own decision.
pat.review-duty-with-a-built-in-exit.fix: Make the review mandatory and require a published reason for any extension.
pat.power-to-exempt-whole-classes.plain: An agency may exempt "any entity or class of entities" on a broad public-interest finding.
pat.power-to-exempt-whole-classes.check: Find powers to exempt 'any entity or class of entities'. Ask what criteria limit the power, and what limits the number or size of the groups exempted.
pat.power-to-exempt-whole-classes.fix: Limit the exemption power by named criteria, time limits and public notice.
pat.unrecorded-waivers-and-exemptions.pl: Waivers are granted with no public record of how many or to whom.
pat.unrecorded-waivers-and-exemptions.ch: Look for a public record of waivers and exemptions. Ask whether anyone can learn how many were granted and to whom.
pat.unrecorded-waivers-and-exemptions.fi: Require a public register (a published list) of each waiver, and an annual report.
pat.narrowing-or-deferral-after-enactmen: Regulations issued under a general grant of power narrow what the statute covers, or a later amendment postpones duties before they apply.
Find general grants of rulemaking power and the risk of later amendment. Ask whether regulations could narrow the statute, or a later law could postpone duties before they apply.
Set the core terms in the statute and add a reporting duty on any narrowing or deferral.
pat.agency-barred-from-supplying-a-defin: Congress blocks the agency from issuing the rule that would supply the definition the text lacks.
Find limits on the agency's power to issue rules. Ask what is left undefined as a result, and who supplies the missing definition.
State the definition in the bill, or allow a narrow rule to supply it.
A review body can only recommend, or an inspector can be removed without notice and reasons.
Find review bodies and inspectors. Ask whether they can only recommend, and whether removal needs notice and reasons.
Give the body binding duties to follow up, and require notice and reasons for removal.
pat.structural-checks-that-can-stall-the: Quorum rules (the minimum number of members needed to act) or supermajority rules let unfilled seats halt the agency's work.
Find quorum and supermajority rules. Ask whether unfilled seats could halt the agency, and what substitute rule applies.
Add a substitute rule for when there is no quorum, and a deadline for filling seats.
pat.deadline-that-distorts-priorities.pl: A rigid deadline or automatic default forces action on one duty at the cost of rushed rules or neglect of others.
pat.deadline-that-distorts-priorities.ch: Find rigid deadlines and automatic defaults. Ask whether they could force action on one duty at the cost of rushed rules or neglect of others.
pat.deadline-that-distorts-priorities.fi: Set priorities among duties and allow a stated extension with reasons.
pat.many-independent-clearance-points.pl: Many separate sign-offs are required before action can be taken.
pat.many-independent-clearance-points.ch: Count the separate sign offs required before action can be taken. Ask whether any one of them can block action, and whether a time limit applies to each.
pat.many-independent-clearance-points.fi: Reduce the number of approvals, set a time limit for each and add a default if one is missed.
pat.administrative-burden-on-beneficiari: Paperwork and other burdens keep eligible people from a right or benefit that exists in the law's text but is hard to claim.
Trace the steps a person must take to claim a right or benefit. Ask how much paperwork and delay is involved, and who bears the cost.
Simplify the process, allow automatic enrollment where possible, and require reporting on how many eligible people take up the benefit.
No clause requires a review against the bill's purpose or secures the data needed to do it, and any review is done by the implementing body.
Look for a clause requiring review against the stated purpose and securing the data needed to do it. Ask who performs the review.
Add an independent evaluation duty with a data plan and a published report.
pat.powers-never-commenced-or-used.plain: Authority is granted but never brought into operation, and no duty requires a report on why.
pat.powers-never-commenced-or-used.check: Find powers that need a start date or a first act. Ask whether any duty requires them to be brought into operation or reported on if not used.
pat.powers-never-commenced-or-used.fix: Add a commencement date and a duty to report why any power has not been used.
pat.reform-that-codifies-existing-practi: A new rule would have changed almost no past cases.
Compare the new rule with current practice. Ask how many past cases it would have changed.
Add a measurable change or a review of whether the rule alters practice.
pat.committee-review-bypassed.plain: Text passes under emergency or leadership procedure, or a draft is enacted without the expected stage for correcting technical errors.
pat.committee-review-bypassed.check: Check how the text moved through the process. Ask whether it passed under emergency or leadership procedure, and whether the stage for correcting technical errors was skipped.
pat.committee-review-bypassed.fix: Require committee review and a posting period before the full chamber acts, and a technical review of the final text.
pat.externally-drafted-or-model-text.pla: Bill text is drafted by an outside organization or copied closely from one.
pat.externally-drafted-or-model-text.che: Compare the text with outside documents. Ask whether it was drafted by or copied from an outside organization, and whether that is disclosed.
pat.externally-drafted-or-model-text.fix: Require disclosure of outside drafters and a review of the text against the bill's purpose.
A board's or official's recommendation takes effect unless Congress acts to stop it.
Find recommendations that take effect unless the legislature acts. Ask who can stop them, how quickly, and what happens if no one does.
Require an affirmative approval step, or a clear time window and procedure for disapproval.
pat.expedited-procedure-that-limits-amen: Expedited procedures restrict debate and amendment.
Find expedited procedures. Ask what debate and amendment they allow, and what changes could not be made.
Allow amendment and a minimum period of debate, or limit expedited procedure to defined cases.
pat.authority-to-skip-public-comment.pla: Rules can take effect before or without public comment through good-cause exceptions, interim final rules or guidance documents.
pat.authority-to-skip-public-comment.che: Find routes that allow rules to take effect without comment, such as good cause or interim final rules. Ask what limits them.
pat.authority-to-skip-public-comment.fix: Limit skipping comment to stated circumstances, set an end date on interim rules, and require notice and comment later.
pat.no-comparative-print.plain: The bill is drafted so that no document shows how it changes existing law.
pat.no-comparative-print.check: Look for a document showing how the bill changes existing law. Ask whether readers can see the changes without assembling them.
pat.no-comparative-print.fix: Require a comparative print to be published before consideration.
pat.no-cost-or-regulatory-impact-stateme: The report that accompanies the bill lacks a cost estimate or regulatory impact evaluation.
Look for a cost estimate and a regulatory impact evaluation with the bill. Ask who prepared them and whether they cover the main provisions.
Require a cost estimate and impact evaluation before consideration.
pat.no-agency-technical-review.plain: The bill was drafted without technical assistance from the agency that will administer it.
pat.no-agency-technical-review.check: Look for technical assistance from the agency that will administer the bill. Ask whether the text was reviewed for workability.
pat.no-agency-technical-review.fix: Request and publish a technical review from the administering agency before enactment.
pat.provision-added-or-dropped-late.plai: A safeguard, a corrective provision or a protective provision is added to or removed from a must-pass bill late in the process.
pat.provision-added-or-dropped-late.chec: Compare earlier versions of the bill with the final text. Ask what was added or removed late, especially safeguards, corrective provisions and protective provisions.
pat.provision-added-or-dropped-late.fix: Require a posting period for late changes and a record of what was added or dropped.
pat.drafting-and-reading-conventions-dif: Drafters do not follow several canons (rules of interpretation) that courts apply, so text is read in ways its authors did not expect.
Compare the drafting style with the canons courts apply. Ask where the text could be read in ways its authors did not expect.
Have the text reviewed against common interpretive canons and add construction rules where they differ.
pat.procedure-that-favors-a-constituency: Procedural rules give particular groups special access to information, the right to sue, or chances to block action.
Read procedural rules for who receives information, the right to sue, or chances to block action. Ask whether a particular group gains an advantage.
Open procedural rights to all affected parties, and require public notice of key steps.
rules.inq.obligation.0: What has the party that holds the discretion actually done with it, under this bill or under the closest earlier law?
rules.inq.obligation.1: Look for the official's own stated reading, instances where the power went unused or was used against its purpose, and who was affected and how many.
rules.inq.obligation.2: Agency court filings and guidance; GAO and inspector general reports; oversight letters; news investigations
rules.inq.definitions.0: Which people or things fall just outside each defined or limiting term?
rules.inq.definitions.1: Look for specific entities, products, record types or people on each side of each term's boundary, and existing statutory definitions that could be borrowed.
rules.inq.definitions.2: U.S. Code definitions; agency rules; case law on the term; industry filings
rules.inq.actors.0: Who else holds the authority, the records or the capability, and are they bound by the bill?
rules.inq.actors.1: Look for agencies and components by name, contractors, levels of government, and what each is documented to hold or do.
rules.inq.actors.2: Agency records libraries and FOIA logs; GAO; committee letters; earlier statutes with wider scope
rules.inq.timing.0: What happened at the bill's deadline, or at similar deadlines in other laws?
rules.inq.timing.1: Look for dates met and missed, what followed, and who could act when the date passed.
rules.inq.timing.2: Court dockets; the Unified Agenda; GAO deadline reviews; contemporaneous reporting
rules.inq.exceptions.0: Who has used the bill's exception, or a similar exception in another law, how often, and for what purpose?
rules.inq.exceptions.1: Look for uses of the exception with counts and dates, and the stated ground compared with the apparent use.
rules.inq.exceptions.2: Transparency reports; inspector general audits; annual FOIA reports; litigation records
rules.inq.enforcement.0: What happened when someone tried to enforce this provision, or a provision built the same way?
rules.inq.enforcement.1: Look for cases, courts, holdings and dates, who had standing (the right to sue), and which remedy was available and which was refused.
rules.inq.enforcement.2: Dockets and opinions; Justice Department filings; enforcement records under parallel statutes
rules.inq.money.0: What was appropriated against what was authorized, and who ended up paying?
rules.inq.money.1: Look for dollar amounts by fiscal year and account, unfunded duties, and who bore the cost.
rules.inq.money.2: Appropriations acts and reports; CBO estimates; USAspending; GAO
rules.inq.delegation.0: What must an agency do before the bill's provision takes effect, and has the agency done it?
rules.inq.delegation.1: Look for rulemakings by docket, standards bodies and their members, advisory panel rosters, and the time that has elapsed.
rules.inq.delegation.2: Federal Register; regulations.gov; advisory committee records; ACUS studies
rules.inq.information.0: Who receives the information that the bill requires to be reported, is it public, and can anyone check it?
rules.inq.information.1: Look for reports filed and not filed, recipients, what was blacked out, and who audited.
rules.inq.information.2: Committee sites; agency report pages; GAO; press comparison of promised and delivered disclosures
rules.inq.interaction.0: Which existing laws govern the same conduct, and which one prevails?
rules.inq.interaction.1: Look for sections by citation with the standard each applies, the volume of use, and which is specific and which is general.
rules.inq.interaction.2: U.S. Code; CRS reports; case law on implied repeal and preemption
rules.inq.constitutional.0: Which constitutional doctrine has been used against provisions built like this one, and with what result?
rules.inq.constitutional.1: Look for cases with holdings, and the feature of the provision that drew the challenge.
rules.inq.constitutional.2: Constitution Annotated; Supreme Court and appellate opinions; CRS legal sidebars
rules.inq.symbolic.0: What happened to this text procedurally, and which binding bills or laws exist or would be needed?
rules.inq.symbolic.1: Look for introductions, cosponsor counts, votes, and companion bills and their status.
rules.inq.symbolic.2: Congress.gov actions; roll call records; CRS on forms of legislation
rules.inq.evidence.0: Who measures compliance, with what data and baseline, and can the party being measured shape the result?
rules.inq.evidence.1: Look for datasets, methods and thresholds, who supplies the data, and known disputes about the measure.
rules.inq.evidence.2: Agency methodology documents; GAO; academic critiques
rules.inq.market.0: Which firms fall on each side of each threshold, and who gains from where it is set?
rules.inq.market.1: Look for firms by name with their size against the threshold, market shares, and who sought the provision.
rules.inq.market.2: Securities filings; FTC and agency studies; lobbying disclosures
rules.inq.process.0: How did the text change between versions, and who sought the change?
rules.inq.process.1: Look for differences from version to version, amendments and sponsors, and registered lobbying on the provision.
rules.inq.process.2: Congress.gov text versions; Congressional Record; Lobbying Disclosure Act filings
rules.inq.mechanics.0: How have courts read a sentence built this way, and which reading helps which party?
rules.inq.mechanics.1: Look for the competing readings in plain words, the canon (interpretive rule) each relies on, and a decided case with the same sentence shape.
rules.inq.mechanics.2: Supreme Court and appellate opinions; the CRS canon list; the House and Senate drafting manuals
rules.inq.response.0: What is the cheapest change in form, structure or timing that takes a regulated party outside the bill's rule?
rules.inq.response.1: Look for the specific restructuring, split, relabeling or substitute, and who has already announced or used it.
rules.inq.response.2: Law firm and accounting firm client alerts; trade press; agency notices closing or confirming a route; tax scholarship
rules.inq.design.0: Has a program built this way worked, and what did auditors find?
rules.inq.design.1: Look for the comparable program, the audit finding, and numbers for participation, error or fraud.
rules.inq.design.2: GAO and inspector general reports; implementation studies; state sunset reviews
rules.cand.0.1: A party can restructure an activity so that a lighter set of rules applies.
rules.cand.1.1: Parties dispute which legal category an actor falls in, such as employee, bank or broker.
rules.cand.1.2: Tax Notes; labor and financial regulation case studies
rules.cand.2.1: Actors stay just under a size trigger, or split themselves to do so.
rules.cand.3.1: A law lets the agency waive the law's own core requirements.
rules.cand.4.1: An agency declines to enforce a law as a way of changing the law in practice.
rules.cand.4.2: Inspector general reports; administrative law journals
rules.cand.5.1: Sunsets and phase-ins are arranged to meet a cost estimate.
rules.cand.6.1: Text is enacted through omnibus or emergency measures with no committee process.
rules.cand.7.1: Outside experts identify errors while a bill is moving through Congress.
rules.cand.8.1: Since 2024, courts and not agencies resolve statutory ambiguity, which changes the effect of vague delegations of power to agencies.
rules.cand.9.1: The regulated agency helps draft its own constraints
rules.cand.10.1: This topic covers fee shifting, bounties and citizen suits, and what happens when they are absent.
rules.cand.11.1: Some deadlines carry an automatic consequence, and other deadlines do not.
rules.cand.12.1: Courts have formally reported drafting problems to Congress.
rules.mech.open_term.1: A broad open term reaches actors, technologies and situations the drafters did not foresee. A list or tight definition can leave something out, and what is left out is presumed excluded.
rules.mech.open_term.2: Whoever first applies an open term can choose a narrow reading. Disputes then take years, and different courts can read the term differently.
rules.mech.open_term.3: Who interprets an open term first, and does that person or body share the measure's purpose? Is the risk of leaving a case out larger than the risk of a narrow reading?
rules.mech.discretion.1: Discretion lets the official fit the rule to the facts, protect third parties case by case, and avoid absurd mandatory results.
rules.mech.discretion.2: A reluctant official can decline to act, and no one can compel a choice that the law left open.
rules.mech.discretion.3: Is the official who holds the discretion someone the measure relies on, or someone the measure is aimed at?
rules.mech.feasibility.1: A feasibility limit avoids commanding the impossible and makes the provision harder to strike down.
rules.mech.feasibility.2: A feasibility limit sets the standard by evidence about what is feasible, and that evidence usually comes from the regulated party.
rules.mech.feasibility.3: Who must prove what is feasible, and who checks the claim?
rules.mech.exception.1: An exception, waiver or safe harbor protects legitimate cases such as emergencies, victims and small actors, rewards good-faith compliance, and can be a concession needed for the measure to pass.
rules.mech.exception.2: Exceptions grow, and the party that the rule constrains is usually the one that invokes them.
rules.mech.exception.3: Who invokes the exception, is each use counted and reviewed, and does the exception expire?
rules.mech.threshold.1: A threshold spares small actors and concentrates enforcement where the risk is.
rules.mech.threshold.2: Actors restructure to stay under the threshold, and a fixed threshold becomes outdated as markets and technology change.
rules.mech.threshold.3: How cheaply can someone split or restructure to get under the threshold, and is the threshold indexed or aggregated?
rules.mech.timing.1: A delay, phase-in, sunset or grandfathering gives time to comply, forces Congress to revisit an untested policy, and protects those who relied on the old rule.
rules.mech.timing.2: A delay can end up working as a repeal, a sunset creates a sudden end date that others can exploit, and grandfathering gives existing parties a lasting advantage.
rules.mech.timing.3: What happens by default when the date in the bill arrives and no one acts?
rules.mech.delegation.0: Delegation to an agency or outside body
rules.mech.delegation.1: A delegation brings expertise and lets the rule keep pace with change without new legislation.
rules.mech.delegation.2: The agency can delay or come under the control of the interests it regulates, and since 2024 courts, not agencies, resolve statutory ambiguity.
rules.mech.delegation.3: Is there a deadline with a default rule if the agency does nothing, and who are the members of the body?
rules.mech.remedy_limit.1: A limit on enforcement or remedies prevents opportunistic lawsuits, keeps enforcement consistent and protects public funds.
rules.mech.remedy_limit.2: A right without a remedy depends on an enforcer who may lack resources, independence or interest.
rules.mech.remedy_limit.3: Does the body that can enforce have the means and the motive to do it?
rules.mech.narrow_scope.1: A narrow scope is easier to pass, clear about who is responsible, and less exposed to constitutional challenge.
rules.mech.narrow_scope.2: The activity or the records can move to parties that the measure does not cover.
rules.mech.narrow_scope.3: How easily can the conduct shift outside the measure's scope?
rules.mech.preempt.1: One national rule lowers compliance cost and prevents conflicting obligations.
rules.mech.preempt.2: A federal minimum standard can become the maximum allowed and displace stronger state protections.
rules.mech.preempt.3: Does the measure set a minimum standard or a maximum standard, and what state law does it displace today?
rules.mech.confidentiality.1: Confidentiality protects victims, security and legitimate commercial secrets.
rules.mech.confidentiality.2: The same confidentiality protection can cover the conduct that the measure is meant to expose.
rules.mech.confidentiality.3: Who reviews a claim of confidentiality, and can they see the material?
rules.mech.symbolic.1: A non-binding statement, study or report builds a record and a coalition, signals direction, and gathers evidence before a mandate.
rules.mech.symbolic.2: A non-binding statement, study or report can stand in for action and be presented as if a step had been taken.
rules.mech.symbolic.3: Is there a binding companion measure, or a trigger that turns the study into a duty?
rules.mech.funding_flex.1: Leaving funding to later decisions keeps annual control over spending and lets funding track results.
rules.mech.funding_flex.2: A duty without money does not get carried out, and funding decisions can become a quiet way to repeal a duty.
rules.mech.funding_flex.3: Is the duty conditioned on funding, and what happens in a year with none?
rules.mech.measurement.1: A simple metric can be administered easily and compared across cases.
rules.mech.measurement.2: The measured party learns to satisfy the metric without achieving the goal.
rules.mech.measurement.3: Who supplies the data, and can the method be changed without notice?
rules.standards.0.who: House Office of the Legislative Counsel
rules.standards.0.says: The House manual says to use the present tense, singular and active voice, "may" for a power, "shall" for a duty and "may not" for a prohibition. It says to discourage findings and purposes (sec. 325). It also says a severability clause is unnecessary unless it says in detail which provisions would fall if a court strikes down another (sec. 328).
rules.standards.1.who: House Office of the Legislative Counsel
rules.standards.1.says: This manual states the rule for text inside quotation marks in amendments, and the rule on citing positive law titles.
rules.standards.2.who: House Office of the Legislative Counsel
rules.standards.2.says: This short guide sets out House drafting conventions and was revised 10 June 2026.
rules.standards.3.who: House Office of the Legislative Counsel
rules.standards.3.says: This document lists questions for drafters. They ask to whom the policy applies, what exceptions exist, who carries it out, "What if the policy is not followed?", whether penalties are civil or criminal, how much lead time is needed, and whether transitional rules are required.
rules.standards.4.who: Senate Office of the Legislative Counsel
rules.standards.4.says: The Senate manual says "'And/or' has not gained acceptance in legislative drafting" (sec. 302), and "Avoid the use of 'notwithstanding any other provision of law'" (sec. 314). It also says a severability clause "is unnecessary" (sec. 131), and that a sunset of authority does not repeal amendments the Act made (sec. 127).
rules.standards.5.who: Congress, codified by the Office of the Law Revision Counsel
rules.standards.5.says: Default meanings apply unless the context indicates otherwise: singular includes plural, present tense includes the future, and "person" includes corporations. Each section should contain, as nearly as may be, a single proposition of enactment, and a repealed Act is not revived by repeal of the repealer unless expressly provided.
rules.standards.6.who: Office of the Law Revision Counsel
rules.standards.6.says: The office explains that a positive law title is amended directly, while a title that is not positive law is amended through the underlying Act.
rules.standards.7.says: House rules require a committee report to print the text of each section to be repealed and "a comparative print of each amendment".
rules.standards.8.says: These House rules contain the Cordon rule, require a cost estimate and a regulatory impact evaluation in committee reports, bar general legislation on appropriations bills, and confine conference committee members to matter committed to them.
rules.standards.9.who: U.S. Senate, as described by the Congressional Research Service
rules.standards.9.says: Under Senate rules, a reconciliation provision is extraneous on six grounds, including one that it "does not produce a change in outlays or revenues".
rules.standards.10.says: Agency legislative proposals must include a section-by-section analysis and budget and personnel impacts, and spending authority outside regular appropriations, called backdoor financing, is limited.
rules.standards.11.says: This guidance covers executive agency documents only, excludes regulations and bars judicial review of compliance, so it does not apply to bills.
rules.standards.12.says: These rules govern documents published in the Federal Register.
rules.standards.13.says: The President directs executive drafters to state limitations periods, preemptive effect, retroactivity, burdens of proof and key definitions in clear language.
rules.standards.14.says: The guide says "Do NOT use 'shall' or 'must' to state a rule of law" and "Do not include substantive provisions in a definition."
rules.standards.15.who: UK Office of the Parliamentary Counsel
rules.standards.15.says: The guide avoids the legislative "shall", warns against "sandwich" provisions and mixed conjunctions, and says to add "or both" where "or" is inclusive.
rules.standards.16.says: The joint guide bars circular and serial references, requires a static reference to say so, and bars autonomous substantive provisions inside amending acts.
rules.standards.17.says: The guide adds subject-specific directions on offences, regulatory powers, evidence and conferral of powers. Only titles and dates were confirmed.
rules.conflicts.0.says: Include a clear severability clause (also add severability for litigation-friendly drafting).
rules.conflicts.0.but: Both the Senate and House manuals call a general severability clause unnecessary because courts presume severability. The better practice is a specific nonseverability clause or fallback for provisions that form a package.
rules.conflicts.0.src: Senate manual sec. 131; HOLC manual sec. 328
rules.conflicts.1.says: Add a rule that lists are illustrative, using "including but not limited to" as the wording that signals this.
rules.conflicts.1.but: Both manuals say "includes" already signals a partial list and "but is not limited to" is redundant. The risk they identify is "means" used where an open list was intended.
rules.conflicts.2.says: Include specific findings, specific findings on scope, and a statement that purposes guide interpretation.
rules.conflicts.2.but: The House Office of the Legislative Counsel (HOLC) manual sec. 325 says to discourage findings and purposes, though HOLC and the Senate manual accept findings that help establish congressional power or clarity, and the ADA has an enacted rule of construction.
rules.conflicts.3.but: Under TransUnion v. Ramirez, Congress may not relieve federal courts of deciding whether a plaintiff has a concrete harm, so a statutory grant of standing does not by itself let the plaintiff sue in federal court.
rules.conflicts.4.says: Add meaningful penalties, enforcement funding and a private right of action.
rules.conflicts.4.but: The Congressional Research Service (CRS) documents three limits. Civil penalties imposed in an agency tribunal face the Jarkesy jury-trial holding, statutory damages without concrete harm face TransUnion, and rights created by spending statutes need rights-creating terms after Medina.
rules.conflicts.5.says: Rely on an independent regulator or assessor assumed to be protected from removal.
rules.conflicts.5.but: The Congressional Research Service (CRS) reports that Trump v. Slaughter (29 June 2026) overruled Humphrey's Executor and held Federal Trade Commission commissioners removable at will, with Federal Reserve governors treated separately.
rules.conflicts.6.says: Provide a dedicated funding source and pair authorizations with mandatory funding.
rules.conflicts.6.but: The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) episode shows the limit. The 2025 law cut the funding cap from 12 to 6.5 percent, and the Bureau declined to request funds until a court ruled. The Office of Management and Budget's A-19 and the manuals also disagree on "such sums as may be necessary".
rules.conflicts.7.says: Add a default rule or a right to sue when a deadline is missed.
rules.conflicts.7.but: The Congressional Research Service (CRS) describes such automatic consequences as self-enforcing but warns of hastily imposed rules. Administrative Conference of the United States (ACUS) Recommendation 78-3 says Congress ordinarily should not impose statutory time limits on rulemaking.
rules.conflicts.8.says: Treat "reasonable" or "appropriate" as a weakness and give express discretion to the agency.
rules.conflicts.8.but: Loper Bright recognizes that a statute may expressly delegate definitional authority or leave agencies flexibility, citing enacted formulas such as "as such terms are defined and delimited by regulations of the Secretary".
